claims.subject: engine/plan/target.ts
claims.value: Declared Intent — not Outbound Artifacts

evidence.note: The standing 'Outbound Artifacts' cluster groups this with render/mermaid.ts as two ways of getting the map out. The file itself makes the opposite claim: it is 'the shape the code is *supposed* to have... the one thing no amount of extraction can derive — it is intent, so a human or an agent declares it and it lives with the repo.' TargetSpec is an INPUT authored alongside the code, not an artifact emitted from it. mermaid.ts takes a Graph and returns a string; this takes a declaration and diffs reality against it.

The invariants loader makes the identical argument in the identical shape — 'invariants belong to the repo being analysed, not to this tool... they are authored and live with the code they constrain' — and is currently in a different cluster ('Invariant Check'). Two files asserting the same principle about the same class of artifact are one subsystem; the current cut splits them and instead pairs one with a diagram printer.

Counter-evidence that 'Outbound Artifacts' is not a subsystem at all: its other member disavows itself as a stopgap whose mechanism is to be replaced ('already a focus operation, and a crude one: it elides by path depth, which is a filing decision rather than an intent claim'). A cluster whose stated purpose is carried by a diagram printer and a declaration format is grouping by the direction data happens to flow, which is a filing decision — the same error the mermaid header names.

clusters.purpose: Hold every capability the window is not allowed to have. The renderer displays agent-authored text, so it is treated as untrusted: no filesystem, no spawn, no store — only named operations this process validates, runs and reports back.

evidence.note: "Holds the data, owns every job, and hardens the renderer. The renderer displays agent-authored text (cluster names, purposes, elision reasons), which is untrusted content, so: contextIsolation on, nodeIntegration off, a narrow preload surface, no remote content, no navigation."

"Jobs shell out to `node src/cli.ts` rather than importing the TypeScript directly — one implementation of every operation" — this process deliberately holds no engine code, which is what makes it a capability boundary rather than a second copy of the product
the entire renderer API is a list of invoke() wrappers over named ipc channels — arbitrate is one line, and anything not on this list is unreachable from the window by construction

clusters.name: Invariant Check
clusters.purpose: Make the top of the map falsifiable: compile the prose facts a human would hand-write into queries against L0 that re-run every pass, and keep those facts in the repo they describe so no codebase is ever measured against another's architecture.

evidence.note: An invariant is a query against L0; prose and compiled form live in one object so they cannot drift apart.
Predicate union: absent / count / literal-fanin / forbidden-call — prose facts as graph queries.
Shipping a fixed set marks every other codebase STALE against facts that were never about it.
l3Status is derived from invariant results — this is what makes L3 checkable rather than asserted.

clusters.name: Belief and Provenance
clusters.purpose: Accumulate every assertion about the map alongside who made it and what they cited, and keep disagreement alive rather than resolving it — a contradiction is this system's highest-value output, not an error state.

evidence.note: "Every interesting assertion about the graph lives here with its provenance, and nothing is ever overwritten — disagreement is preserved, not resolved."

the polarity rule was DISCOVERED by running two models on the same questions: naive value-inequality gets it backwards, since two prose purposes always differ textually (loud false contradictions) while `duplicates` vs `not_duplicates` never gets compared at all. Narrative predicates corroborate; verdict predicates normalise onto one predicate with a boolean.
the POLARITY table is where a real disagreement becomes machine-visible — is_dead/partially_dead/not_dead/is_live all collapse onto liveness_verdict

clusters.name: Spatial Memory
clusters.purpose: Give the graph a body you can fly and navigate back to from memory — position is a pure function of the focus stack with no solver and no randomness, and camera distance IS altitude, so pulling back collapses a node into its agent-named abstraction instead of fading it out.

evidence.note: the consumer states the two properties the whole node exists for: "the spine is a pure function of the focus stack (no force relaxation, no randomness, so flying around builds spatial memory), and LOD is SEMANTIC — camera distance IS altitude on the focus stack, so pulling back collapses nodes into their agent-named abstraction rather than fading them out"

Scene.tsx imports layout and layoutTree across the app/engine boundary — the geometry is engine code and the panel is its dumb consumer, so cutting this cluster on the app/ vs engine/ folder line would split one mechanism in half

the cone tree exists because the focus stack's three flat buckets throw the real nesting away; it is "deterministic, like the graph layout — the same repo lays out the same way every session, which is the whole basis for spatial memory"

the belief palette encodes the same epistemic stance as the store: UNKNOWN is deliberately near-invisible so "an unexamined map should look unexamined" — colour here is a claim about knowledge, not styling

clusters.name: Ground Truth
clusters.purpose: Turn a repo that may not compile into one exhaustive, content-addressed graph stated in a vocabulary that never names a language — so every claim made above it resolves back to a span, and the language that produced a fact is a swappable provider rather than a property of the map.

evidence.note: "L0 graph — the exhaustive layer. Everything above it is derived by recorded elision. Language-neutral on purpose: a parser provider fills these in, and nothing here mentions TypeScript."
contentHash on every node is declared as the invalidation key — the content-addressing is in the vocabulary itself, not a caching detail bolted on later

declares the Parser contract (name, extensions, parse(relPath, source, contentHash)) and states that import-specifier resolution happens OUTSIDE the parser — which is why resolve.ts is a separate global pass rather than parser-internal

clusters.name: Arbitration Surface
clusters.purpose: Where the human closes the stigmergic loop: read what the swarm deposited, see precisely where two sources disagree, and issue the CONFIRMED verdict that outranks every agent and actually removes things from the map.

evidence.note: "The arbitration surface — the screen the design calls the highest-value thing in the product, and which until now was a JSON file. Contradictions first, because a disagreement between two sources is worth more than another unexamined node." The default filter is literally 'contradicted'.
"Pick the claim that is right — that becomes CONFIRMED and outranks every agent" — the panel states the authority ordering the whole belief calculus rests on

the tab set is not five screens, it is one loop: "a running agent is quiet most of the time... the honest signal is 'how long since anything happened', not 'nothing is happening'" — this exists so the human can tell a working swarm from a dead one before judging what it deposited

the store is snapshotted before every job "so completion can report the delta rather than making you read a log to find out what happened" — the window is built to surface what changed for judgement, not to browse

clusters.name: Ground Truth
clusters.purpose: Turn an unbuildable, half-written repo into the one exhaustive L0 graph that every later claim must resolve back to — syntactically, so broken code still maps, and content-addressed, so an unchanged file is never parsed twice.

evidence.note: L0 is the exhaustive layer; everything above is derived by recorded elision. Language-neutral on purpose.
Deliberately syntactic: no type info, no node_modules walk — resolves what a bundler would for first-party code.
Parsing is the expensive half and is per-file content-addressed; resolution stays global and re-runs.
looksVendored: vendored bundles are not authored code and wreck every downstream number.
ParsedFile is the provider contract — providers report what was written, resolution happens outside.

clusters.name: Composition Root
clusters.purpose: Own the only path from a request to a finished artifact — every operation the product performs is wired exactly once here, so the window and the terminal cannot drift, and the outward forms of the map are produced nowhere else.

evidence.note: every operation the product performs is a case in one switch here — map, extract, invariants, focus, derive, plan, query, arbitrate, agent — including the arbitrate path the GUI reaches only by shelling out to this file
confirms the seam from the other side: the Electron ipc handler for vds:arbitrate spawns this CLI with 'arbitrate' rather than importing the engine, so the GUI and the terminal run identical code

mermaid is the map's cheapest outward form and is explicitly a stopgap whose mechanism M1.5 replaces — it is an output format of the composition root, not a subsystem standing beside Ground Truth and the Agent Plane

clusters.name: Declared Intent
clusters.purpose: Hold the one thing extraction can never derive — what this code is SUPPOSED to be — as machine-checkable declarations that live in the repo they constrain, and express the gap against L0 as either a failing fact or an ordered plan with blast radius attached.

evidence.note: "Invariants belong to the repo being analysed, not to this tool... shipping a fixed set and running it everywhere marks every other codebase STALE against facts that were never about it. They are authored and live with the code they constrain."

Same argument, different artifact: "the shape the code is *supposed* to have. This is the one thing no amount of extraction can derive — it is intent, so a human or an agent declares it and it lives with the repo. Everything else here is a diff against that declaration." And what it adds over ArchUnit/Sonargraph is that violations become an ordered plan, not a flat rule-failure list.
Violation.count is documented as "the weight of the problem" — blast radius is a field on the diff, not a presentation choice

clusters.name: Silent-Failure Gates
clusters.purpose: Pin the three things in this system that go wrong without throwing — evidence enforcement at the agent boundary, the polarity of the belief calculus, and the referent rule in the geometry — because the failure mode here is not a crash, it is a confident-looking map that is quietly false.

evidence.note: drives createServer over an in-memory transport against ClaimStore to exercise the EvidenceRequired boundary — an unevidenced write must be rejected, and nothing else in the system would notice if it stopped being

merges two agent runs through canonicalise/ClaimStore and asserts corroboration vs CONTRADICTED — the polarity rule is the one correction that turned the contradiction queue from noise back into signal, and getting it backwards produces a plausible queue, not an error

imports layoutTree and checks the referent rule in geometry — fake trunks, phantom strata, nodes visible but not hoverable — which is exactly the class of defect that pixel-hunting in a screenshot cannot catch

clusters.name: Candidate Findings
clusters.purpose: Propose — never decide — the specific ways this codebase is redundant or misshapen, emitting tiered candidates that carry their own caveat, because a confident wrong finding is worse than none: it is the one that gets acted on.

evidence.note: every dead-code result is a DeadCandidate carrying a confidence tier and a `why` explaining why it is not a higher tier, because static reachability is wrong in exactly the ways real codebases are built — dynamic dispatch, DI, file-based routing, decorators, plugin registries, string-keyed lookups; the header states the thesis: the detector proposes, an agent or human adjudicates

duplication is emitted as families of candidates for adjudication rather than as a verdict — the overview counts one duplicationFamily, and the store's polarity table carries duplicates/not_duplicates precisely because this output is expected to be argued with

clusters.name: Altitude Control
clusters.purpose: Decide what survives at each altitude and keep the collapse lossy rather than a lie — every node enumerates its members, a defended node is never moved, and an elision whose target does not resolve is rejected out loud instead of conjuring a subsystem that does not exist.

evidence.note: members is non-optional on a focus node, so a node that cannot enumerate what it stands for cannot be constructed; defended nodes are filtered out of every elision before it applies; an elision whose target resolves to neither a cluster nor a module group is reported as rejected rather than creating the bucket; a human CONFIRMED-false verdict actually removes a cluster

negative evidence for why this cluster is a subsystem and not a folder: the mermaid path-depth grouping is called out in its own header as "already a focus operation, and a crude one: it elides by path depth, which is a filing decision rather than an intent claim" — focus/ exists precisely to replace that mechanism with recorded, attributable elisions

clusters.name: Outbound Artifacts
clusters.purpose: Get the map out of the tool and into work someone can act on — a diagram cheap enough to paste into a PR or an agent's context, and the gap between declared intent and actual wiring expressed as ranked steps with blast radius attached.

evidence.note: The target is the one thing no extraction can derive; what this adds over ArchUnit is that violations become an ordered plan with blast radius.
L1 render — a crude focus operation kept so the output stays comparable to the hand-drawn map.
taskPackets are written to disk as step-N.md — self-contained prompts, the second export path.
Design names exactly these two as the exports: Mermaid for parity/PRs, task packets to make execution trivial.

clusters.name: Agent Plane
clusters.purpose: Rent judgment from external agent CLIs and let it back in only as evidenced claims — aim each sandboxed, read-only run at the most uncertain-and-central open question, and make one stdio boundary the only write path that exists.

evidence.note: "score = uncertainty x centrality... Resolving a hub changes more downstream beliefs than resolving a leaf, and a contradiction is worth more than a blank. The queue drains when the top score falls below a floor — that is the natural 'the map has converged' signal, rather than an arbitrary iteration count." The aiming is a scheduler, not a loop.

SYSTEM_RULES hands every rented agent the same posture: READ-ONLY, "the ONLY thing that counts is the tool calls you make against the 'vds' MCP server", every claim needs evidence because "a claim without evidence is rejected at the boundary", and a purpose is intent, not a file list

the driver resolves mcp/server.ts as SERVER_ENTRY and hands out serverCommand() — the four adapters and the evidence boundary are one mechanism, so splitting swarm/ from mcp/ would put the enforcement in a different subsystem from the thing it enforces on

clusters.name: Composition Root
clusters.purpose: Own the only path from a request to a finished artifact — every operation the product performs exists exactly once here, so the window and the terminal cannot drift, and the outward forms of the map are produced nowhere else.

evidence.note: runMap is the one-pass ordering: a single extract feeds the detectors, the invariant evaluation and the focus stack. The individual subcommands re-parse; this is the only place the pass is composed.
runDerive rebuilds the whole stack from cached graph.json with no re-extraction — the operation that makes a continuously-live map affordable.
The GUI deliberately shells out to engine/cli.ts rather than importing the engine, so there is exactly one implementation of every operation. CLI is a resolved path constant, not a module import.
The only import of render/mermaid.ts anywhere in the repo — verified by grep across ts/tsx/cjs.
The only import of plan/target.ts anywhere in the repo — verified by grep across ts/tsx/cjs.
The outward form that carries intent: declared target architecture diffed into ranked steps with blast radius, emitted for a person or an agent to act on.
The cheap outward form: an L1 render whose own header calls it a crude focus operation kept for comparability, superseded by recorded agent-proposed elisions.

elisions.reason: vite.config.ts is the build of the window the host serves: it sets root to app/renderer and base './' precisely because production loads the renderer over the custom app:// scheme the main process registers. A one-file build config standing as a peer of Ground Truth and the Agent Plane asserts a subsystem that does not exist — it is a property of the capability root, not a thing beside it.

Outbound Artifacts is grouped by output shape, not by intent, and neither member has an independent existence: engine/render/mermaid.ts and engine/plan/target.ts are each imported by exactly one file in the repo, engine/cli.ts (cli.ts:8, cli.ts:15 — verified by grep, no other importer). A pair whose sole consumer is the command that invokes them is the tail of that command, not a peer subsystem of Ground Truth and the Agent Plane. Collapsing them also removes the one architecture-level node still labelled by a directory: engine/cli.ts currently stands at L3 as the raw path group "engine", which is a filing decision masquerading as intent — precisely what this level is supposed to eliminate. mermaid.ts argues its own case here: its header describes an L1 render kept only so the early milestone produced something comparable to the hand-drawn map, explicitly superseded by recorded agent-proposed elisions. Net effect at L3: eleven nodes to ten, and every survivor named by what it is for.

At architecture altitude a gate belongs with the thing it holds honest, not in a box labelled 'tests'. Both files exist only to exercise the belief calculus and the evidence boundary: smoke.ts drives createServer over an in-memory transport against ClaimStore so an unevidenced write is rejected, and merge-beliefs.ts merges two agent runs through canonicalise/ClaimStore to check corroboration vs CONTRADICTED. Neither is a subsystem; each is the falsifiability of the claim store, and shown beside it they make the store's central claim — disagreement is preserved, not resolved — checkable rather than asserted.

vite.config.ts is the build of the window the host serves: it sets root to app/renderer and base './' precisely because production loads the renderer over the custom app:// scheme the main process registers, which is part of the same no-remote-content posture. A one-file build config standing as a peer of Ground Truth and the Agent Plane asserts a subsystem that does not exist — it is a property of the capability root, not a thing beside it.

An 'Outbound Artifacts' node reads as a subsystem for getting the map out, but mermaid.ts is one function that groups files by path depth and prints a diagram — and its own header disavows the mechanism: 'already a focus operation, and a crude one: it elides by path depth, which is a filing decision rather than an intent claim', kept only until recorded elisions replace it. At architecture altitude it is an output format of the single place every operation is wired, and pairing it there also stops it from being mistaken for a second, competing focus mechanism alongside Altitude Control. The other half of the old pairing, plan/target.ts, belongs with Declared Intent instead — it is a diff against a declaration, not a rendering.

graph/types.ts is pure vocabulary — type declarations with no behaviour, no I/O and no runtime presence. Its very high fan-in is an argument for eliding it, not against: a node that every other node depends on equally adds no information at architecture altitude, it just draws nine edges to itself and makes the level look more coupled than it is. It is the schema of the exhaustive parse, so it belongs to the layer that produces it. The property worth preserving — that detectors, focus, invariants and plan read this vocabulary and never touch a parser — survives as Ground Truth's stated purpose and is enforced structurally inside the cluster by extract/parser.ts, which is defended separately for exactly that reason.

Same argument, different subject: scene.ts imports layoutTree and exists solely because the layouts are where the referent rule keeps getting violated — fake trunks, phantom strata, nodes visible but not hoverable — and pixel-hunting in screenshots cannot catch that. It is the check on the geometry, so it collapses into the geometry rather than standing beside it. With this and the two store gates elided, 'Silent-Failure Gates' correctly ceases to exist at L3: it was never a subsystem, it was three files each belonging to a different one.

defences.reason: Defended against my own collapse instinct, because this is the cheapest remaining way to take L3 from ten nodes to nine and it is the wrong one. Scene.tsx is a tab in App.tsx, rendered by the same React root as Review and Findings, so on a dependency graph Spatial Memory and Arbitration Surface look like one window that got cut in half. They are not the same claim. Arbitration Surface exists so a human can issue a verdict; this node exists so the map has a body that is the same body every session — position is a pure function of the focus stack, no force relaxation, no randomness, and camera distance IS altitude rather than a zoom level. Two structural facts make the separation real rather than aesthetic. First, the mechanism is engine code: layout.ts and tree.ts hold no React and no THREE, are consumed identically by the standalone geometry check, and Scene.tsx imports them across the app/engine boundary — collapsing this into the renderer would file a deterministic, testable pure function under "the GUI" and invite the next person to reach for a force pass to fix an overlap. Second, layout.ts is already a defended node, so this collapse would be filtered down to moving three files while leaving the defended one stranded beside them — a merge that buys no simplification and costs the reader the reason the remaining node is there. The failure mode is the whole argument: a jittering layout still renders. Nothing throws, no correctness test fails, the screenshot looks right, and the only symptom is that the user's memory of where a subsystem sits stops working across sessions. That regression is invisible in exactly the medium people would review it in, so the map has to name it at the altitude where someone decides what this view is for.

Trust boundary. This 51-line file IS the entire capability surface between agent-authored text rendered in the window and a process holding fs, spawn and the claim store. Every capability the renderer has is one of the named operations listed here; anything not on this list is unreachable by construction. Collapsing it into 'the Electron app' erases where the trust boundary sits, which is the one thing a security reader opens this map to find.

Argued against the direction I pushed everywhere else in this pass, and against the obvious read of it: this looks like drawing code, the softest thing on the level, and Spatial Memory would seem to lose nothing by collapsing to "the 3D view". It should survive, because the determinism is not a rendering detail — it is the entire product claim of the view. "The layout is DETERMINISTIC. Flying around only builds spatial memory if the same repo lays out the same way every session, so there is no force relaxation and no randomness here — position is a pure function of the focus stack." Purity is asserted in this one file and enforced nowhere else: hashAngle derives the angular seed from a stable content hash so subtree ordering never jitters, and LEVEL_Y/LEVEL_RADIUS are fixed tables rather than a solver's output. That is why Scene.tsx can be a dumb consumer of it, and why the standalone check on the geometry was collapsed into this node rather than kept beside it. The failure mode is the reason to defend it: a jittering layout still renders. Nothing throws, no test of correctness fails, the screenshot looks fine, and the only symptom is that the user's memory of where a subsystem sits stops working over sessions — a regression that is invisible in exactly the medium people would try to review it in. Anyone adding a force pass or a Math.random tiebreak to fix an overlap would be destroying the feature while appearing to polish it, and at architecture altitude this node is the only place the map says so.

Argued against my own instinct to collapse. Candidate Findings and Ground Truth look like one node from a distance: both are deterministic, both run with no LLM and no spend, both read only the Graph, and both write into the same findings/graph pair that cli.ts emits in a single pass. Merging them would take L3 from ten nodes to nine, which is the direction this level is supposed to move. It is still wrong, and this file is why. Ground Truth asserts fact — an exhaustive, content-addressed parse where every node resolves back to a span. This file asserts guesses, on purpose: every dead-code result is a DeadCandidate carrying a confidence tier and a `why` explaining why it is not a higher tier, because static reachability is wrong in exactly the ways real codebases are built — dynamic dispatch, DI, file-based routing, decorators, plugin registries, string-keyed lookups. Its header states the product thesis outright: the detector proposes and an agent or human adjudicates, because a confident dead-code report is worse than none, since it gets acted on. Putting a tiered guess in the same architecture-level box as an exhaustive parse erases the epistemic difference the whole belief calculus exists to preserve, and the failure it invites is the one this tool is built to prevent — a caveat dropping off a finding on its way to being acted on. The boundary between what was measured and what was inferred must be visible at the altitude where someone decides to trust the map.

Sole write path, and the single point where evidence is enforced. Agents read the repo with their own tools but can only affect the map through a tool on this server, and every write tool requires a non-empty evidence array at the schema boundary (EvidenceSchema, .min(1)). It is also the one place all four adapters converge — the events.jsonl the GUI tails is written here because the CLIs stream differently. If it disappears into 'Agent Plane', the map stops asserting the property the whole design rests on: that a confabulated claim cannot get in.

Hub and single source of belief. focus/stack.ts, swarm/frontier.ts, swarm/driver.ts, mcp/server.ts and cli.ts all import it — highest fan-in in the engine — and it is the only place contradiction is preserved rather than resolved. Its polarity rules (narrative predicates corroborate, verdict predicates normalise onto a boolean) are the correction that turned the contradiction queue from noise back into signal. Eliding it hides both the fan-in and the one invariant that makes the map arguable.

Outbound trust boundary, and the counterweight to the defence already standing on mcp/server.ts. server.ts guards what comes back IN — no claim without evidence. This file is the only place anything goes OUT: the sole spawn of an external agent binary in the engine, and the only place the read-only posture is actually asserted rather than assumed. Every constraint that keeps a rented agent from mutating the repo is a literal in this one file and nowhere else — claude's --allowedTools list naming eleven read/query tools and no write tool, codex's -s read-only, grok's --tools read,grep,glob,ls, the stated rule that no adapter ever passes --dangerously-*, --always-approve or --auto, and the refusal to run `mcp add` on the user's behalf because it would silently mutate their config (registrationHint prints the command instead). The header records that these flags were verified against the installed binaries rather than recalled, which is exactly the kind of fact that decays silently. It is also the only spawn site that hard-kills on timeout (SIGTERM then SIGKILL at 5s) and refuses a shell even for `which`. Collapsed into Agent Plane it sits beside frontier.ts, a pure scoring function with no I/O at all, and the map stops showing where the sandbox is declared — which is the first thing anyone auditing an agent harness opens it to find, and the first thing to quietly regress when a fifth adapter is added.

The provider seam, and the only thing standing between this map and the false claim that this is a TypeScript tool. 48 lines, no runtime code — which is exactly why it is the first thing an eye looking for subsystems will discard into "Ground Truth = the parse", and that collapse would be lossy in the one direction that matters. Parser (name, extensions, parse(relPath, source, contentHash) -> ParsedFile) is a contract, and ts-parser.ts is one implementation of it, not the thing itself. The split is load-bearing in a way the file makes explicit: "Resolution of import specifiers to files happens outside the parser — providers only report what was written." That single sentence is what keeps a new language provider from having to reimplement module resolution, and it is the reason resolve.ts is a separate global pass rather than parser-internal. Nothing downstream of extract/ imports ts-parser.ts; everything reads the graph vocabulary instead, so the swappability is real today, not aspirational. Its failure mode is silent and structural: the second provider gets added by copying the TypeScript one and leaning on some TS-shaped assumption that leaked past the interface, and the graph quietly stops being language-neutral while every downstream consumer keeps compiling. Ground Truth's whole claim is that a fact resolves back to a span regardless of what produced it — this file is where that regardless is written down, so it cannot be invisible inside the cluster that claims it.

Counterweight to my own elisions: this one looks small (2 files, 51 symbols) and reads like a helper of the focus stack, since l3Status is computed from its results. It should still survive. It is the only mechanism that makes a claim at the top of the map falsifiable from the bottom, it runs with no LLM and no agent spend at all — so it is the tool's standalone value — and its failure mode is specifically the one this product exists to prevent: a map that has quietly gone stale. Eliding it into Altitude Control would render the status without rendering what produces it.

The only place human authority enters this system, and the top of the belief hierarchy. Arbitration Surface is eight files and the obvious next collapse is "the window" — five tabs, one React app. That collapse would be wrong, and this file is why. Every other tab reads; this one writes a verdict that outranks every agent, and the map says so in its own words: "Pick the claim that is right — that becomes CONFIRMED and outranks every agent" (line 189). A CONFIRMED-false verdict issued here is the only input that makes focus/stack.ts actually remove a cluster, so it is the sole path by which anything an agent proposed can be taken back out of the map. Its second property is just as load-bearing and even easier to lose: contradictions are the default filter, not a tab you find (line 10), because "a disagreement between two sources is worth more than another unexamined node" — the screen is ordered by the design's own claim about where value is. Structurally it is also the counterpart to the two boundaries already defended: mcp/server.ts is where agent claims get in under evidence, adapters.ts is where agent runs go out under sandbox, and this is where a human overrules both. A map that shows the two machine boundaries but hides the human one describes an autonomous system, which is precisely the thing this product is not. The failure mode is quiet: strip the arbitration buttons and everything still renders, the swarm still deposits, the store still accumulates — the tool just silently becomes unfalsifiable by its user, with agent consensus as the highest available authority.

This is where the referent rule is enforced structurally rather than by review: members is non-optional so a node that cannot enumerate its members cannot be constructed, defended nodes are filtered out of every elision before it applies, an elision whose target resolves to neither a cluster nor a module group is rejected and reported instead of conjuring a bucket, and a human CONFIRMED-false verdict actually removes a cluster. Every past incident where the map lied — phantom subsystems, the fake trunk — is now prevented in this file. It cannot be inside the thing it polices.

Composition root and the seam between the two front ends. Every operation the product can perform — map, extract, invariants, focus, derive, plan, query, arbitrate, agent — exists once, here, and the Electron main process deliberately shells out to this file rather than importing the engine, so the GUI and the terminal run identical code. It is also where the one-pass ordering lives (runMap: one extract feeding detectors, invariants and the focus stack) and where derive re-builds the stack from cached graph.json with no re-parse, which is what makes the live map affordable. Collapse it and the map loses the fact that there is only one implementation.
